facts.title: Named for Russia
facts.text: Ruthenium takes its name from Ruthenia, the Latin word for Russia, honoring the region where its ores were found. It was isolated in 1844 by the Russian chemist Karl Ernst Claus, who worked at the University of Kazan. Claus famously confirmed the new metal's existence partly by tasting and smelling its compounds, a practice no chemist would recommend today.

facts.title: The last platinum metal found
facts.text: Ruthenium was the final member of the six platinum-group metals to be discovered, completing the set that includes platinum, palladium, rhodium, osmium, and iridium. Earlier chemists had glimpsed hints of it: Jędrzej Śniadecki claimed a metal he called 'vestium' in 1807, and Berzelius and Osann investigated platinum residues in the 1820s. Claus's careful work in 1844 finally proved it was a genuine, distinct element.

facts.title: Rare beyond imagination
facts.text: Ruthenium is one of the scarcest stable elements in Earth's crust, present at roughly one part per billion by mass. Annual world production is only around 20 to 30 tonnes, most of it recovered as a byproduct of nickel and platinum mining in South Africa's Bushveld Complex. Because it is so concentrated in ores from a few places, its supply is geographically very limited.

facts.title: A metal that resists almost everything
facts.text: Ruthenium does not dissolve in ordinary acids, not even in aqua regia, the potent mix of nitric and hydrochloric acid that attacks gold. It is also extremely hard and brittle, which makes pure ruthenium difficult to machine. To chemically attack it, you typically need an oxidizing molten alkali, showing just how inert this metal is under normal conditions.

facts.title: It toughens jewelry and pen nibs
facts.text: Adding just a small percentage of ruthenium to platinum or palladium dramatically increases their hardness and wear resistance. This is why ruthenium-platinum alloys appear in high-end jewelry and in the hard-wearing tips of fountain pen nibs. The same property made ruthenium valuable for durable electrical contacts that must survive millions of switching cycles.

facts.title: Hidden inside your hard drive
facts.text: Ruthenium played a key role in expanding computer storage through a technique sometimes nicknamed 'pixie dust.' An ultrathin ruthenium layer, only about three atoms thick, is sandwiched between magnetic films to couple them in a way that lets data be packed far more densely. IBM introduced this antiferromagnetic coupling layer in 2001, helping push hard-disk capacities sharply higher.

facts.title: A Nobel-winning catalyst
facts.text: Ruthenium sits at the heart of the Grubbs catalysts, ruthenium complexes that revolutionized a reaction called olefin metathesis, which lets chemists efficiently rearrange carbon-carbon double bonds. Robert Grubbs shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this work, alongside Yves Chauvin and Richard Schrock. These catalysts are now used to build everything from pharmaceuticals to advanced plastics.

facts.title: Solar power and dye cells
facts.text: Ruthenium-based dyes were central to the dye-sensitized solar cell invented by Michael Grätzel in the early 1990s. In these cells, a ruthenium complex absorbs sunlight and injects electrons into a titanium dioxide film, mimicking part of how plants capture light. The approach offered a cheaper, flexible alternative to conventional silicon panels and inspired a whole field of research.

facts.title: Eight bonds in one compound
facts.text: Ruthenium can reach an unusually high oxidation state of +8 in the molecule ruthenium tetroxide, RuO4. This volatile, golden-yellow compound is a powerful oxidizer and is used in the lab to cleave double bonds and even to stain biological samples for electron microscopy. Its +8 state ties it with osmium and a few others for the highest oxidation numbers any element is known to reach.

facts.title: Fighting cancer with metal
facts.text: Because ruthenium compounds interact with biological molecules differently than platinum-based drugs, they have become promising candidates in cancer research. Experimental agents such as NAMI-A and BOLD-100 have advanced into clinical trials, designed to slow tumor spread or kill cancer cells with potentially fewer side effects than cisplatin. Ruthenium's ability to mimic iron in the body may help these drugs reach tumors selectively.
